items.title: Dave Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Wilton, Connecticut, November 21, 2001
items.q: And Art Tatum — there’s never been anybody yet with his ability... And he had command of the harmonic and rhythmic ideas more than anybody I’ve ever known.

ctx.x: Yeah. Neither was Louis Armstrong. And Garner, who is one of my favorites, was — he didn’t know about reading, didn’t need to know and didn’t care. So how did he develop you know. He was perfection. And Art Tatum — there’s never been anybody yet with his ability, and yet he was a person that didn’t read, he just heard and produced and wrote — not wrote, he played. And he had command of the harmonic and rhythmic ideas more than anybody I’ve ever known. And there’s people like George Shearing that, it’s amazing,…
Yeah. When you go to compose a new piece, does it usually come from a commission that has some guidelines for what they want? A subject area perhaps?

items.title: Dave Brubeck — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Why wouldn’t you call Art Tatum’s Elegy or Humoresque . . .

ctx.x: A few years after you began mixing jazz and classical music, a term came about called “Third Stream.” People would talk about Third Stream, sort of a blending between jazz and classical. Did you feel like you were part of that movement? Or did you feel that was something very similar to what you were doing? Or that came after you? What was your reaction to the Third Stream?

Gunther [Schuller]’s such a brilliant musician that I respect him. If he uses the term “Third Stream,” it’s probably correct for what he wants to express. But I think that Jelly Roll Morton was listening to the music from the French opera house quite often, and that they’re just discovering things of Jelly Roll that were never published or no-one else was too familiar with until recently. I’d like to hear what Jelly was doing. I would say that there’s certain influences in jazz. Why wouldn’t you call Art Tatum’s…
